headline: Forget the Fluke Grind — the Bunker Pods Off Short Beach Are Where the Smart Money's At
subhead: While the bay crowd chases scattered fluke on warm mud, the real action is topwater on bait pods and a building tide that's about to get a lot stronger.
body_markdown:
Every boat coming off the ramp this week wants to talk fluke, and every one of them is telling me the same thing — soft bite, fish scattered, marks all over the sounder but nobody biting with any conviction. I'm not surprised. That flat mud on the inside of the bay has been sitting in warm, thin water for two weeks straight, and fluke don't concentrate in that garbage — they spread out and sulk. If that's all you're fishing, you're fishing the wrong program right now.

Here's what I'd be doing instead: working the bunker pods stacking along Jones Beach and off Short Beach on the calm mornings, because that's where the next move is coming from. The bait's been thick off the beach for going on two weeks, rolling in tight, nervous balls right off the second bar, and where you've got bait like that stacked up in late August, you've got fish watching it — even in a stretch where the striper bite inside is supposed to be dead.

And let's be honest about that inside bite — it is a summer lull, not a fall run. The stripers sitting in Hempstead Bay and around the inlet structure right now are holding, not migrating, and they'll stay in that lazy pattern until the nights start cooling off for real, which is probably three weeks out yet. That means daytime bass fishing inside the bay is going to keep being tough sledding — small windows, mostly night-bite guys working the bridge lights and the channel edges after dark. But the ocean side, where that bait is stacked, is a different animal entirely, and that's the disconnect nobody's talking about.

We flagged this a few days back — said the moon building toward full would tighten up the tidal flow and sharpen the dawn and dusk windows at the inlet, and that's exactly what's setting up now with the full moon hitting the 28th. Tide swings are already noticeably stronger than they were a week ago, and that means more water moving through the inlet on the last two hours of the ebb and the first hour of the flood — which is when the current edges off the jetty rocks and the deeper cuts in the main channel start holding fish tight instead of scattered.

The fluke that are biting are coming off the channel edges where that moving water keeps a cooler bottom layer alive — the drop along Sloop Channel and the deeper stretch off the West End are still worth a drift, especially on the last of the outgoing when the current is still hauling bait off the flats. White Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow right on bottom, are outfishing bare bucktails and definitely outfishing bait sitters — the fish that are there want something moving, not something sitting dead in warm water. Depths of 15 to 25 feet along that channel edge have been the sweet spot; go shallower than that and you're back in the soft, spread-out bite everybody's complaining about.

Bluefish are still the one thing you can count on inside the bay right now. Snappers are thick around the Wantagh Bridge pilings and up into the Freeport creeks, and cocktail-class blues to three or four pounds are mixing right in with the fluke catches on the channel drifts — same bucktails, same depth, no extra work required. If you've got kids or you just want bent rods without overthinking it, that's your play.

Weakfish are the sleeper story this month, and the shop talk backs it up — a scattered but real showing of legal-sized weakfish coming out of the deeper holes in the bay on incoming water, mostly on soft plastics fished slow near bottom, sometimes on bait if you've got fresh peeler crab or bloodworms. It's not a sure thing, and it's not everywhere, but it's more consistent than it's been in a couple of seasons, and worth a look on the same tide stage that's been producing the fluke.

On the ocean side, the beach bite is going to be the story to watch over the next several days. With bunker still stacking off Short Beach and the stretch of Jones Beach toward the Coast Guard station, calm mornings before the wind builds are the window — topwater plugs and big soft-plastic swimbaits worked right through the edge of the bait balls have a shot at connecting with the bass and blues shadowing those pods, even in a lull month. It won't be every morning. Wind out of the southwest kills it fast once it builds past ten or twelve knots, which has been the pattern most afternoons.

Looking ahead, the full moon on the 28th should keep tightening those tide swings through the weekend, and that's good news for the inlet structure — expect the dawn and last-light windows at the jetty rocks and the main channel drop to keep sharpening as the extra water moves through. If you've only got one shot this week, take it on a moving tide at first light, work the bait if you see it stacked off the beach, and fall back to the channel edges with bucktails if the surface stays quiet. That's the honest read — not everything's biting, but there's enough here to make the trip worth planning around the tide, not just the calendar.
